image.caption: First page of the Popol Vuh in Francisco Ximénez's copy, early 18th century (Newberry Library)

versions.title: Viracocha Paints the Nations
versions.teaser: At Tiwanaku, the creator gives every people its language, dress and songs.
versions.text:
The priest Cristóbal de Molina, writing in Cusco around 1575 from the testimony of Inca elders, records how the creator Viracocha remade humanity after a great flood. At Tiwanaku, beside Lake Titicaca, he shaped the peoples out of clay and painted on each the clothing it was to wear. To each nation he gave the language it would speak, the songs it would sing, and the seeds and foods it would sow.

Then he commanded them to go down into the earth, and each emerged in its own homeland, from a cave, a lake, a spring or a hill. That place became its pacarina, its sacred place of origin, and the first ancestors of many peoples were turned to stone or into animals and honoured as huacas.

Here the many tongues of the Andes are not a curse but an ordinance: part of the pattern the creator stamped on the world, each people given its own speech, dress and place.
sources: Cristóbal de Molina, Relación de las fábulas y ritos de los Incas (c. 1575)
versions.caveat: Recorded by a Spanish priest; the flood-and-recreation frame may show some biblical shaping, though the pacarina ideas are well attested.

image.file: File:Bol-tihuanaco-sonnentor.jpg
image.caption: The Gateway of the Sun at Tiwanaku, Bolivia

concepts.summary: A world once free of trouble is spoiled when something is opened, broken or trespassed: a jar, a sealed pit, the boundary of heaven. Pandora is the classic case, though her story is less about female curiosity, the reading that spread in the Renaissance, than about the gods' revenge disguised as a gift. Parallels range from demons escaping a well to diseases invented by wronged animals. They are mostly independent explanations for suffering that share one logic: evil was once contained and now, through a single act, is loose. The details, and where the blame falls, differ widely.

versions.title: Pandora's Jar
versions.teaser: Zeus's lovely gift to humankind lifts a lid and lets out every sorrow.
versions.text:
Angry at Prometheus' theft of fire, Zeus orders a gift for humankind in which they will all delight, embracing their own ruin. Hephaestus shapes a maiden from earth and water; Athena dresses her, Aphrodite gives her grace and longing, and Hermes a shameless mind and a thief's character. She is named Pandora, "all-gifts", and Hermes leads her to Epimetheus, who forgets his brother's warning never to accept a gift from Zeus.

Before this, men lived on earth free of evils, hard labour and sickness. The woman lifts the great lid of a storage jar, a pithos, and scatters its contents. Sorrows spread among humans, and diseases roam by day and night, silently, since Zeus has taken away their voice. Only Hope stays inside, under the rim.

The familiar "box" is a Renaissance slip: Erasmus rendered pithos as pyxis, a small casket, and the image stuck.

image.file: File:John William Waterhouse - Pandora, 1896.jpg
image.caption: John William Waterhouse, Pandora, 1896, showing the Renaissance 'box' rather than Hesiod's jar

versions.title: The Watchers Descend
versions.teaser: Rebel angels come down to earth and teach forbidden arts.
versions.text:
Genesis mentions, in four cryptic verses, that "the sons of God" took human wives and that the Nephilim were on the earth. The Book of the Watchers, the oldest part of 1 Enoch, composed in Aramaic by the third century BCE, turns this into a catastrophe. Two hundred angels, the Watchers, led by Shemihazah, descend on Mount Hermon and bind themselves by oath to take human wives.

They bring forbidden knowledge with them. Asael teaches men to forge swords and armour, and women to make bracelets, ornaments and eye paint; others teach spells, the cutting of roots, astrology and the signs of the moon. Their children, the giants, devour the labour of humans and then humans themselves, and the earth cries out.

God answers with the flood and a prison. Asael is bound hand and foot and cast into darkness in the desert of Dudael, under rough and jagged rocks, until the day of judgement. For this author, war, vanity and sorcery are knowledge that should never have left heaven.
versions.caveat: 1 Enoch lies outside the Hebrew Bible (it is canonical only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church) and expands the brief Genesis passage.

versions.title: The Sun in the Cave
versions.teaser: The storm god's outrages drive the sun into hiding, and calamities swarm.
versions.text:
Having won a contest with his sister Amaterasu, the storm god Susanoo runs riot in heaven. He breaks down the ridges between her rice fields, fills in the irrigation ditches, and defecates in the hall where the first fruits are tasted. At last he breaks a hole in the roof of her sacred weaving hall and drops in a heavenly piebald horse, flayed backwards. A weaving maiden, startled, strikes herself with her shuttle and dies.

Terrified, Amaterasu shuts herself in the Rock Cave of Heaven and closes the door. The Plain of High Heaven and the land below go dark, and endless night reigns. The voices of the myriad gods swarm like flies in summer, and every kind of calamity arises.

Only a riotous dance by the goddess Ame-no-Uzume, the laughter of eight hundred myriad gods, a mirror and a jewelled tree coax the sun back out. Susanoo is fined, his beard and nails are cut, and he is expelled from heaven.

image.file: File:Amaterasu cave - large - 1856.jpeg
image.caption: Utagawa Kunisada, Amaterasu emerging from the Rock Cave of Heaven, 1856

versions.title: Poison from the Ocean
versions.teaser: Churning the sea for immortality, the gods first bring up a world-killing poison.
versions.text:
When the gods and the asuras churn the ocean of milk to win the drink of immortality, they use Mount Mandara as the churning stick and the serpent Vāsuki as the rope. The first thing the ocean yields is not treasure but a deadly poison, Hālāhala, which spreads in every direction, choking all living things.

Gods, demons and creatures flee to Śiva for help. Out of compassion, and with the approval of his wife, he gathers the poison into his palm and swallows it. It does him no harm, but it stains his throat dark blue, and he is called Nīlakaṇṭha, "Blue-Throat", ever after. Only then can the churning go on to bring up the wish-granting cow, the white horse, the goddess Lakṣmī, and at last the physician Dhanvantari carrying the pot of amṛta.

The story reverses Pandora's order. The evil comes out first, and is swallowed, so that the good things can follow.

image.file: File:Churning of the Ocean of Milk at Tonle Bati.jpg
image.caption: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk, Khmer relief at Tonle Bati, Cambodia

versions.title: Ahriman Breaks In
versions.teaser: Roused by a demoness, the Evil Spirit bursts into the perfect creation.
versions.text:
For three thousand years, the Bundahishn relates, Ahriman lies stunned in the darkness, overwhelmed by Ohrmazd's recitation of the Ahuna Vairya prayer. His demons try to rouse him and fail. At last the demoness Jeh comes and cries out: rise, our father, for I will pour so much affliction on the Righteous Man and the toiling bull that life will not be worth living. Ahriman is delighted and kisses her head.

Then he leaps. He springs through the sky like a snake, at noon, and invades the whole good creation: salt and bitterness in the water, noxious creatures on the earth, poison in the plants, smoke in the fire, and death for the bull and for Gayōmard. From that moment the world is a mixture of good and evil, a battleground that will remain so until the final Renovation.

The Zoroastrian answer to suffering is stark: nothing in the world was made to be evil; everything evil in it broke in from outside.
versions.caveat: The Bundahishn was compiled in the ninth century CE, though it draws on much older tradition.

versions.title: The Hundred and Eight Stars
versions.teaser: An arrogant official opens a sealed pit and releases a hundred and eight spirits.
versions.text:
The fourteenth-century novel Water Margin opens with a warning against meddling. A plague sweeps the Song empire, and the emperor sends Marshal Hong Xin to Dragon and Tiger Mountain to summon the Daoist Celestial Master for rites. While there, the arrogant marshal comes upon a locked hall, the Hall for Subduing Demons, its doors pasted over with talismanic seals.

He forces the priests to open it. Inside stands a stone tablet on a tortoise's back, inscribed with the words "Open upon meeting Hong." Delighted to find his name, Hong has the tablet dug up. Beneath it is a deep pit, and from it a black vapour roars up into the sky and scatters into a hundred golden lights. The horrified priests explain that thirty-six Heavenly Spirits and seventy-two Earthly Fiends had been imprisoned there since the Tang.

The released stars are reborn as the hundred and eight outlaws of Liangshan Marsh, whose rebellion fills the rest of the novel.
versions.caveat: A literary novel rather than a religious myth, though it draws on Daoist ideas of star spirits.

versions.title: Loviatar's Nine Sons
versions.teaser: The blind daughter of Death gives birth to the diseases.
versions.text:
In the forty-fifth rune of the Kalevala, Louhi, mistress of the North, avenges the theft of the Sampo by sending diseases against the people of Kaleva. Their mother is Loviatar, blind daughter of Tuoni, lord of the dead, the worst and most wicked of his daughters.

Loviatar lies down with her back to the wind, and the east wind makes her pregnant. Her labour drags on for months, and at last Louhi takes her to a sauna in the North, where she gives birth to nine sons, each a disease: pleurisy and colic, gout and consumption, sores, scab, canker and plague among them. The ninth is left without a name and sent off to work mischief in the swamps. The rest Louhi sends against Kaleva, and the people fall sick.

Väinämöinen heats the sauna, prepares ointments and sings his charms, and drives the diseases away to the Mountain of Pain, where they can trouble no one.
versions.caveat: The Kalevala is Lönnrot's nineteenth-century compilation, but it draws here on genuine Finnish charms describing the diseases as Loviatar's offspring.

versions.title: The Animals Invent Disease
versions.teaser: Hunted without respect, the animals hold councils and devise human illnesses.
versions.text:
In the old days, the Cherokee say, humans and animals lived together in friendship. But people multiplied, invented bows, blowguns, knives and hooks, and began to slaughter the larger animals for their flesh and skins and to trample the smaller ones carelessly underfoot.

The animals held councils to take revenge. The Bears, meeting in their townhouse under Kuwâ'hï mountain, tried to make bows of their own, but a bear's claws spoil the shot. The Deer decided that any hunter who killed a deer without asking its pardon would be struck with rheumatism. The Fishes and Reptiles sent dreams of snakes and rotting fish. Then the Birds, Insects and small animals met with the Grubworm presiding, and named disease after disease; the Grubworm was so pleased that he fell over backward, and has wriggled on his back ever since.

When the Plants heard, they took pity on humans. Each tree, shrub and herb agreed to provide a cure for one of the diseases.
sources: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900)

concepts.summary: Flood stories are among the most widespread of all myths, but they are not all one story. The Mesopotamian account, in which a god warns one man to build a boat, birds are sent out and a sacrifice follows, is almost certainly the ancestor of the biblical Noah and may have shaped Greek Deucalion; the Indian Manu story may belong to the same wider orbit. Elsewhere, from China to the Andes, flood myths look independent: responses to real floods, to seashells found on mountains, or to the idea that a world must be washed before it is remade. Missionary retelling has blurred some records.

versions.title: Utnapishtim's Ark
versions.teaser: A god whispers to a reed wall, and one man builds a boat.
versions.text:
In Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, Utnapishtim tells how the great gods decided to send a flood. The wise god Ea speaks not to him but to the reed wall of his house: man of Shuruppak, tear down your house and build a boat; abandon wealth and save life.

He builds a vessel as wide as it is long, with six decks dividing it into seven levels, sealed with bitumen, and loads it with his family, craftsmen, animals and the seed of all living things. The storm rages for six days and seven nights. The gods themselves cower like dogs against the wall of heaven, and the mother goddess wails for her people. On the seventh day the sea grows calm, and the boat grounds on Mount Nimush.

He sends out a dove, which comes back; a swallow, which comes back; then a raven, which finds food and does not return. The story is older than the epic: it is taken from the Babylonian poem of Atrahasis.

image.file: File:British Museum Flood Tablet.jpg
image.caption: The Flood Tablet, Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, 7th century BCE (British Museum)

versions.title: Manu and the Fish
versions.teaser: A little fish Manu saves grows huge and tows his ship to safety.
versions.text:
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa tells it plainly. One morning, as Manu washes his hands, a small fish comes into them and speaks: "Rear me, and I will save you." From what? "A flood will carry away all these creatures; I will save you from that." Keep me in a jar, it says, then in a pit, and at last in the sea.

Manu does so. The fish grows into a great fish and tells him the year of the flood, and Manu builds a ship. When the waters rise, Manu ties the ship's rope to the fish's horn, and it carries him over the northern mountain. There it tells him to tie the ship to a tree and to follow the water down as it sinks. The slope is still called Manu's Descent.

The flood sweeps away all creatures; Manu alone remains. He pours offerings of butter, sour milk, whey and curds into the waters, and a year later a woman rises from them, Iḍā, through whom he begets humankind.

image.file: File:Matsya and Manu.jpg
image.caption: Vishnu as Matsya towing Manu's boat, Mewar painting, c. 1840

versions.title: Noah's Ark
versions.teaser: One righteous man, an ark of gopher wood, a dove with an olive leaf.
versions.text:
Seeing that the earth is corrupt and full of violence, God regrets having made humankind and resolves to blot it out. Noah alone finds favour. He is told to build an ark of gopher wood, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide and thirty high, coated with pitch inside and out, and to bring aboard his family and pairs of every living creature.

The fountains of the great deep burst open and the windows of heaven are opened. The waters rise above the highest mountains, and everything on dry land with the breath of life dies. The ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven, then a dove, which comes back; the second time it returns with a fresh olive leaf, and the third time it does not return.

Noah builds an altar and sacrifices, and God smells the pleasing odour and promises never again to curse the ground. The parallels with Gilgamesh, down to the birds and the aroma, are unmistakable.

versions.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha
versions.teaser: Two survivors repopulate the world by throwing stones over their shoulders.
versions.text:
Zeus, disgusted with the men of the bronze age, or in Ovid's version with the savagery of King Lycaon, who served him human flesh, resolves to destroy humankind by flood. Prometheus warns his son Deucalion, who builds a chest, stocks it with provisions and embarks with his wife Pyrrha, daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora.

Zeus pours rain from heaven and floods most of Greece; all perish except a few who escape to the high mountains. Deucalion's chest floats for nine days and nights and comes to rest on Parnassus. When the rain stops, he sacrifices to Zeus, who lets him ask for whatever he wishes, and he asks for people.

In Ovid, the oracle of Themis tells the pair to throw the bones of their great mother behind them. Pyrrha is horrified, until Deucalion understands: the earth is their mother, and stones are her bones. The stones he throws become men, Pyrrha's women, and so, Greek writers noted, a people, laos, came from stones, laas.

image.file: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Deucalion and Pyrrha, 1636.jpg
image.caption: Peter Paul Rubens, Deucalion and Pyrrha, 1636 (Museo del Prado)

versions.title: Yu Tames the Waters
versions.teaser: Not a punishment but an engineering problem, solved by a tireless sage.
versions.text:
In Chinese tradition the great flood is not a punishment but a disaster to be managed. In the time of the sage-king Yao, the waters overflow the sky, swallow the hills and surround the mountains. Gun is appointed to control them. According to the Classic of Mountains and Seas, he steals the Lord on High's xirang, a self-growing "swelling soil", to dam the flood without waiting for permission, and is executed at Feather Mountain. From Gun's body, Yu is born.

Yu succeeds where his father failed, not by damming but by dredging: he cuts channels, deepens rivers and leads the waters to the sea. For years he labours away from home, passing his own door three times without going in, until the hair is worn from his shins. Daoist ritual masters still imitate his limping gait, the "Step of Yu".

Having drained the land, Yu divides it into the Nine Provinces and founds the Xia dynasty. The flood myth becomes a charter for the state as engineer.

image.file: File:King Yu of Xia.jpg
image.caption: Ma Lin, Yu the Great, Song dynasty hanging scroll (National Palace Museum, Taipei)

versions.title: Cessair and the Flood
versions.teaser: Ireland's first settlers drown, all but one man who outlives the ages.
versions.text:
The medieval Lebor Gabála Érenn, the "Book of the Taking of Ireland", begins its history before the biblical flood. Cessair, daughter of Bith, son of Noah, is refused a place on the ark, and sets out for the western edge of the world with fifty women and three men: her father Bith, the pilot Ladra, and Fintan mac Bóchra. They reach Ireland forty days before the flood.

The women are divided among the three men. Ladra and Bith soon die, and Fintan, left alone with the whole company, flees. Then the flood comes and drowns everyone in Ireland except Fintan, who survives on a hilltop, in later tellings by turning into a salmon, then an eagle and a hawk, before becoming a man again.

He lives on for thousands of years as Ireland's memory, witnessing each invasion that follows and advising kings long into the Christian era. The native imagination has made room, beside Noah, for a single Irish survivor.
versions.caveat: A medieval Christian synthesis grafting Irish tradition onto biblical history; the compilers themselves were uneasy that Fintan survived a flood meant to spare only Noah's family.

versions.title: The Flood of Ymir's Blood
versions.teaser: The gods kill the first giant, and his blood drowns his kin.
versions.text:
When Odin and his brothers Vili and Vé kill the primeval giant Ymir, Snorri Sturluson relates, so much blood flows from his wounds that it drowns the whole race of frost giants. Only one escapes, Bergelmir, with his wife, by climbing onto his lúðr, a word that may mean a mill frame, a hollowed trunk or a cradle; from them the families of frost giants descend.

The gods then carry Ymir's body into the middle of Ginnungagap and make the world from it: earth from his flesh, rocks from his bones, sea and lakes from his blood, and the sky from his skull, held up at its four corners by dwarfs.

Snorri seems to be building on a stanza of the poem Vafþrúðnismál, in which a giant recalls his earliest memory: when the wise Bergelmir was laid on a lúðr. The poem says nothing about a flood.
versions.caveat: Many scholars think Snorri reshaped the Bergelmir stanza with Noah in mind; it is a flood of blood, not water, and it saves giants, not humans.

versions.title: Tata and Nene
versions.teaser: The only survivors of the water age are turned into dogs for cooking fish.
versions.text:
In the Legend of the Suns, a Nahuatl account written down in 1558, the fourth age of the world, the Sun of Water, ends in a flood. The sky collapses, the waters sweep everything away, and the people become fish.

But Tezcatlipoca warns one couple, Tata and Nene. He tells them to hollow out a great bald cypress and shut themselves inside, and to eat only one ear of maize each. They obey, and they float safely until the waters go down.

When they come out, they see a fish, drill fire and roast it. The star gods Citlalinicue and Citlallatonac, looking down, ask who is making smoke and fouling the heavens. Tezcatlipoca comes down in anger, cuts off the couple's heads and sticks them onto their rumps, and they become the first dogs. The crime was not in surviving the flood, but in lighting a fire without leave.
sources: Legend of the Suns (Leyenda de los Soles, 1558)

versions.title: The Wooden People
versions.teaser: The gods drown their failed creations in resin, and their tools rebel.
versions.text:
In the Popol Vuh, the gods' third attempt at humanity is a people of wood: the men carved from the coral tree, the women from the pith of reeds. They look and speak like people and multiply, but they have no hearts or minds and do not remember their makers.

So Heart of Sky brings a flood upon them, a great downpour of resin falling from the sky, with darkness by day and by night. Monstrous creatures attack them: one gouges out their eyes, another tears off their heads, others devour their flesh and crush their bones. Then their own possessions rise against them. Their grinding stones complain of being ground every day; their dogs, of being beaten and never fed; their pots and griddles and hearthstones burn their faces.

The wooden people run, trying to climb onto houses, into trees, into caves, and are thrown down. Their descendants, the Popol Vuh says, are the monkeys of the forest, which is why monkeys look like people.

versions.title: The Llama's Warning
versions.teaser: A llama foretells the flood, and a fox's tail is dipped black.
versions.text:
The Huarochirí Manuscript, compiled around 1608, preserves a short, vivid flood story from the mountains east of Lima. In ancient times a man was leading his llama to good pasture, but the animal would not eat and lay grieving. The owner, annoyed, threw at it the cob of the maize he was eating. Then the llama spoke: in five days the ocean will overflow, and the whole world will come to an end.

Frightened, the man gathered food and climbed with his llama and his family to the peak of Villca Coto. There they found every kind of animal already crowded together. The sea rose and covered everything except the very summit, and the water came so close that the fox's tail was soaked, which is why foxes' tails are black at the tip.

After five days the waters went down, and from that one man, the manuscript says, all the people of the world descended once again.
versions.caveat: Recorded in a colonial, missionary setting, though the local details, Villca Coto and the fox's tail, are clearly Andean.

concepts.summary: Floods are only one of the gods' weapons. Myths from the Near East to Mexico describe deities who decide, in anger, weariness or pity for the overburdened Earth, to thin or erase humankind with plague, famine, fire, war or a rampaging goddess, and then relent or are tricked into relenting. Recurring motives are noise, overpopulation and ingratitude. The Mesopotamian, Greek and Indian cases may be connected through old routes of exchange or shared inheritance; the Egyptian and Mexican ones grow from their own theologies of cosmic order, in which the world is repeatedly threatened and renewed.

versions.title: Atrahasis and the Plagues
versions.teaser: Humanity's noise keeps Enlil awake, so he tries plague, drought and famine.
versions.text:
In the Old Babylonian poem Atrahasis, humans were created to take over the lesser gods' labour. But after twelve hundred years the land has grown wide and the people numerous, and the land bellows like a bull. Their noise keeps Enlil from sleep. He decides to thin them with disease, and plague is let loose.

The wise Atrahasis appeals to his god Enki, who gives cunning advice: let the people stop worshipping their own gods and bring offerings only to Namtar, the plague god. Namtar withdraws his hand. Six hundred years later the noise returns; Enlil orders drought, and the storm god Adad withholds the rain. Again Enki advises offerings to Adad alone, and the rain returns. A third attempt, a famine enforced across sky, earth and sea, lasts until people serve up their own children as food.

Only when all this fails does Enlil choose the flood. Afterwards the gods add barrenness and a demon who snatches babies, as permanent limits on human numbers.

image.file: File:Babylon Story of the Flood, Tablet containing the Epic of Atrahasis, 1635 BCE, probably from Sipar. Currently at the British Museum.jpg
image.caption: Old Babylonian tablet of Atrahasis, c. 1635 BCE, probably from Sippar (British Museum)

versions.title: Telipinu Vanishes
versions.teaser: An angry god walks out, and the whole world begins to starve.
versions.text:
The Hittite myth of Telipinu begins with a god leaving in a rage. Telipinu, god of farming and fertility, storms off, putting his right shoe on his left foot and his left shoe on his right. He takes the growth of the fields with him, goes off into a meadow, and falls asleep.

At once mist seizes the windows and smoke the house; the logs on the hearth are stifled, and so are the sheep in the fold and the cattle in the pen. The ewe rejects her lamb and the cow her calf. Barley and wheat no longer grow, the mountains and trees dry out, the springs fail. Gods and humans alike begin to starve.

The gods search for him. The eagle cannot find him; the Storm god himself cannot. At last the mother goddess Hannahanna sends a bee, which stings him awake and makes him angrier still. Only the rituals of the goddess Kamrusepa calm him, and his rage is sealed away in bronze vessels in the underworld.
versions.caveat: Telipinu does not set out to destroy humanity; this is a 'vanishing god' myth, but its effect is the same brush with annihilation.

versions.title: The Eye of Ra
versions.teaser: The sun god sends his Eye to slaughter rebels, then saves us with beer.
versions.text:
When the sun god Ra has grown old, his bones silver, his flesh gold, his hair lapis lazuli, humans plot against him. The Book of the Heavenly Cow, inscribed on a gilded shrine of Tutankhamun and in several royal tombs, tells what follows. Ra summons the gods in secret council, and they advise him to send his Eye against the rebels in the form of the goddess Hathor.

She slaughters them in the desert and returns exulting that she has overpowered humankind, and that it was sweet to her heart; so Sekhmet, "the Powerful One", comes into being. Ra, now wishing to spare the rest, has red ochre brought from Elephantine, ground and mixed into seven thousand jars of beer, which are poured over the fields by night until they stand three palms deep.

In the morning the goddess sees the red flood, takes it for blood, drinks, and goes home drunk, no longer noticing humankind. Ra, weary, withdraws into the sky on the back of the cow Nut.

image.file: File:Book of the Heavenly Cow KV62.jpg
image.caption: The Heavenly Cow held up by Shu, from the gilded shrine of Tutankhamun, 14th century BCE

versions.title: Sodom and Gomorrah
versions.teaser: Abraham bargains with God, but not even ten righteous men are found.
versions.text:
The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah, Genesis says, is great, and their sin very grave. After three visitors come to Abraham's tent, the LORD reveals that he will go down to see whether the cities have done all that the outcry claims. Abraham does something remarkable: he bargains. "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked? Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" Fifty righteous would save the city; then forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and finally ten. God agrees each time.

Ten are not found. Two angels arrive in Sodom, where the townsmen surround Lot's house demanding the strangers; the angels strike them blind and lead Lot's family out at dawn. The LORD rains sulphur and fire from heaven on the cities and on the whole plain. Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.

Next morning Abraham looks down toward the plain and sees smoke rising from the land like the smoke of a furnace.

image.file: File:John Martin - Sodom and Gomorrah.jpg
image.caption: John Martin, The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, 1852

versions.title: The Plan of Zeus
versions.teaser: The Trojan War was arranged to lighten the Earth of humankind.
versions.text:
A fragment of the lost epic Cypria, quoted by an ancient commentator on the opening lines of the Iliad, explains why the Trojan War happened. There was a time when the countless tribes of men, roaming the land, were weighing down the broad breast of the Earth. Zeus saw it, took pity on her, and resolved in his wise heart to relieve her of mankind by fanning the great strife of the war at Ilion, so that the load might be emptied by death.

The same commentator adds that Zeus first thought of destroying humans with thunderbolts and floods, but Momus, the god of blame, advised a subtler plan: marry the goddess Thetis to a mortal, and father a beautiful daughter. From those came Achilles and Helen, and from them the war.

Read in this light, the Iliad's early phrase "and the plan of Zeus was being fulfilled" turns sinister. The war the heroes die for was a population cull decided in heaven.

versions.title: The Burden of the Earth
versions.teaser: Gods take human birth so a great war can relieve the overburdened Earth.
versions.text:
The Mahābhārata frames its great war in much the same way. In the first book, demons defeated by the gods are reborn on earth as proud and violent kings, multiplying until the Earth cannot bear their weight. Burdened, the goddess Earth goes to Brahmā for help.

Brahmā does not destroy the world directly. He orders the gods to take birth on earth in portions of themselves, so that the oppressive kings can be killed in battle. So the heroes of the epic are divine: Yudhiṣṭhira is born of Dharma, Bhīma of the Wind, Arjuna of Indra, while Kṛṣṇa is Viṣṇu himself. The eighteen-day war at Kurukṣetra, in which almost the entire warrior class dies, is the Earth's relief.

The Bhāgavata Purāṇa repeats the scheme, with Earth appearing before Brahmā as a weeping cow. Scholars have long noted how closely this resembles the Greek Cypria.
versions.caveat: Whether the Greek and Indian 'burden of the Earth' stories are inherited, borrowed or coincidental is unresolved.

versions.title: The Four Suns
versions.teaser: Four worlds before ours ended in jaguars, wind, fire and water.
versions.text:
For the Mexica, the present world is the fifth. Each of the four before it had its own sun, and each ended with the destruction of its people. The Legend of the Suns, written down in 1558, and the Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas give different orders, but the fates are memorable.

In the Legend's order, the people of the sun 4 Jaguar are devoured by jaguars. Those of 4 Wind are swept away by a hurricane and become monkeys. Under 4 Rain, fire rains from the sky and the people become turkeys. Under 4 Water they drown and become fish. Our own sun, 4 Movement, is fated to end in earthquakes and famine.

In the Historia, the endings are driven by the rivalry of Tezcatlipoca and Quetzalcoatl, who knock each other's suns from the sky. The fifth sun rose only after gods threw themselves into the fire at Teotihuacan, and it must be fed with blood to keep it moving, lest this world end too.
sources: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas
